segments.text: Factual matrix The appellant is the tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent- landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954, evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument has arisen).

At the time of the lease the cite12†Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (for short, the cite12†TP Act ), had not been extended to Delhi although, later, on December 1, 1962, the said Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord had been receiving rent from the tenant until the time he filed a petition for eviction (1967), the statute which regulated the right to eviction being the cite20†Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 (59 of 1958) (for short, the cite19†Rent Act ).

The eviction petition set out two grounds out of the many specified in cite21†s. 14 of the Rent Act, viz.,unauthorized sub-letting of a portion of the premises and possession, by the tenant, of alternative accommodation.

But, in the High Court, the appellant-tenant fell back on certain defences grounded on cite13†ss.106 and cite14†111 of the TP Act on the score that no notice to quit had been given, nor notice of forfeiture, as prescribed by those sections. There is no dispute that neither notice to quit nor notice of forfeiture determining the tenancy had been given by the landlord. The core of the controversy thus turns on the need to comply with the requirements of cite13†ss.

106 and/or 111 of the cite12†TP Act and the fatal effect of failure in this behalf. The landlord seeks to break through these defences by urging that the lease has expired by efflux of time limited thereby under s. 111(a) and no notice terminating the tenancy under cite13†s. 106 is needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub-letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise can be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by cite16†s.

111 (g) because the cite12†TP Act , as amended by the cite22†Amending Act of 1929, did not, in terms, apply to the present lease and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience, which alone applied, did not desiderate the technical requirement of a notice in writing of an intention to determine the lease.

The Rent Controller, at the floor level, ordered eviction and the Appellate Tribunal affirmed it, upholding the vice of sub-letting without consent of the landlord in the manner specified in cite23†s. 14(1)(b) as 909 also the disability spelt out in cite23†s. 14(1) (h) on acquiring vacant possession of alternative residence. The resistence founded on the cite12†TP Act was also over-ruled by the appellate Tribunal. But, when the case reached the High Court in second appeal, under cite24†s.

39 of the Rent Act, the learned Single Judge felt that certain points of law spun out of the cite12†TP Act deserved consideration by a Division Bench and referred the appeal for determination accordingly to a larger Bench. The Division Bench which heard the appeal dismissed it but granted a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court under cite17†Art. 133 of the Constitution, restricting it, however, to but one ground urged before it. Shri A. K.

Sen, for the appellant, made a gentle hint that the High Court had heard long arguments in March 1974 but could resolve its doubts to deliver a judgment only in May 1975 so much so the freshness of counsel's submissions might have faded somewhat and so we should have a closer look at his points de hors the judgment under appeal.
